lectures.name: Hematopoiesis
lectures.title: Hematopoiesis, Hemoglobin and RBC Morphology
lectures.framing: Every blood cell comes from one pluripotent stem cell maturing along a fixed sequence in the marrow; knowing that sequence, and what normal RBCs look like, is what lets you read a CBC and a smear.
lectures.keypoints: Only bands and segmented granulocytes normally leave the marrow. Leukemia type tracks the maturation arrest: myeloblast = AML, promyelocyte = APL, none = CML. EPO comes from the kidney, TPO from the liver. α-globin: 2 genes on chr 16; β-globin: 1 gene on chr 11; HbF → HbA by 3-6 months. Smear clues: bite cells = G6PD, schistocytes = MAHA, teardrops = myelofibrosis, rouleaux = myeloma.

blocks.html:
Components of blood
  • Plasma: non-cellular fluid of blood — water, proteins (albumin), coagulation factors, immunoglobulins
  • Serum: the liquid left after blood has clotted (plasma minus coagulation factors and fibrinogen)

blocks.cap: Spun blood: ~55% plasma, ~1% buffy coat (platelets + WBCs), ~44% RBCs.

Normal hematopoiesis
  • Hematopoiesis: creation of all cellular components of blood
  • Sites over development: yolk sac (2-3 wk gestation) → aorta/gonad/mesonephros (AGM) region → liver (5-6 wk) → lymph plexuses/thymus (9 wk) → spleen (16 wk) → bone marrow (after 6 months)
  • Children: marrow in all bones; adults: only the axial skeleton
  • Pluripotent hematopoietic stem cell → committed unipotential progenitor cell, which can form a colony (CFU)

blocks.html:
Hemoglobin
  • Transport protein making up 90% of RBC mass
  • Tetramer: HbA = α2β2; HbF = α2γ2; HbA2 = α2δ2
  • 4 α globins from 2 genes on chromosome 16; 2 β globins from 1 gene on chromosome 11
  • Each globin chain carries a heme (Fe2+ + porphyrin); each Fe2+ binds one O2 → each Hb binds up to 4 O2
  • HbF switches to adult HbA and HbA2 at 3-6 months of life

lectures.name: CBC and Anemias
lectures.title: The CBC and the Coulter Counter
lectures.framing: The CBC is the starting point of every anemia workup: it counts each cell line and, through the Coulter counter, sizes the red cells.
lectures.keypoints: A CBC reports WBC, RBC (Hb, HCT, MCV, RDW) and platelet (count, MPV) values; the differential splits WBCs into five types. The Coulter counter counts cells and derives their size from the electrical pulse each one makes.

blocks.html:
The complete blood count
  • CBC: venous blood sample analysed for its cellular components
  • White cells: leukocyte count (LKC)
  • Red cells: erythrocyte count (ERC), hemoglobin (Hb), hematocrit (HCT), mean cell volume (MCV), RBC distribution width (RDW)
  • Platelets: platelet (thrombocyte) count, mean platelet volume (MPV)
  • CBC + white cell differential (CBC+diff, CBC/D) adds the breakdown: neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils

blocks.cap: A sample CBC/D report: every value is read against its reference range (here low WBC, Hb and platelets with a normal MCV — a pancytopenia).

blocks.html:
The Coulter counter
  • Laboratory instrument that counts blood cells and measures their indices
  • Cells in a conductive liquid are drawn through a small aperture between two electrodes; each cell briefly changes the electrical signal, and the size of the pulse reflects the size of the cell

blocks.cap: Each cell passing the aperture produces one voltage pulse; a large cell gives a taller pulse (C) than a small cell (D).

lectures.name: Approach to Microcytic Anemia
lectures.title: Microcytic Anemia (MCV < 80 fL)
lectures.framing: Microcytosis means hemoglobin synthesis has fallen behind cell division — from too little iron, iron that cannot be used, or too little globin. TAILS names the causes.
lectures.keypoints: TAILS. Iron deficiency: find the source of loss, ↑ RDW and transferrin. Chronic inflammation: hepcidin blocks ferroportin — functional deficiency with ↑ ferritin. Sideroblastic: iron in mitochondria, B6 deficiency, Pappenheimer bodies. Thalassemia is quantitative: β-thal minor ↑ HbA2, major ↑ HbF; α-thal has normal HbA2.

blocks.html:
Mechanism

  • Differential — TAILS: Thalassemia, Anemia of chronic inflammation, Iron deficiency, Lead poisoning, Sideroblastic anemia

lectures.name: Approach to Normocytic Anemia
lectures.title: Normocytic Anemia (MCV 80-100 fL)
lectures.framing: A normal-sized red cell with too few of them means the marrow is losing, failing, suppressed or being outpaced by destruction — ABCD.
lectures.keypoints: ABCD: acute blood loss, bone marrow failure, chronic disease, destruction. PRCA = severe reticulocytopenia; aplastic = pancytopenia with fatty marrow; myelophthisis = leukoerythroblastic film with teardrops. Sickle cell: Glu → Val, hidden by HbF until ~3, penicillin prophylaxis to age 5, hydroxyurea.

blocks.html:
Differential — ABCD
  • Acute blood loss
  • Bone marrow failure — pure red cell aplasia, aplastic anemia, myelophthisis
  • Chronic disease (anemia of chronic inflammation — see microcytic anemia)
  • Destruction — hemolysis (see hemolytic anemia), including sickle cell disease

blocks.html:
Marrow failure: workup and management

(Listed once for the marrow-failure group in the source.)

  • Ix: physical exam — no splenomegaly; CBC; peripheral film; BM aspirate/biopsy
  • Mx: febrile neutropenia → blood products + antibiotics; immunosuppression (antithymocyte globulin, cyclosporine, corticosteroids); BM transplant if eligible

Sickle cell disease (autosomal recessive)
  • β-chain disorder: HbS = Glu → Val; HbC = Glu → Lys → Hb polymerization and adhesion
  • Usually does not present until ~age 3 because HbF protects early
  • Heterozygotes have ↑ malaria resistance
  • Sickle trait (HbAS): monitor for hematuria/glaucoma, severe dehydration, renal medullary carcinoma
  • Disease: chronic organ damage, severity depends on genotype; vaso-occlusive crises (VOC), dactylitis, acute chest syndrome, neuropathy, stroke (CVA)
  • Smear/labs: sickle cells, high HbF
  • Ix: newborn screening, Hb electrophoresis, HPLC
  • Mx: folate; hydroxyurea; manage complications; stem cell transplant; penicillin prophylaxis to age 5; VOC → oxygen, IV fluids, opioids/NSAIDs, treat the trigger

lectures.name: Approach to Macrocytic Anemia
lectures.title: Macrocytic Anemia (MCV > 100 fL)
lectures.framing: Big red cells come either from impaired DNA synthesis (B12/folate — megaloblastic) or from membrane and counting effects (liver, reticulocytes, clumping, thyroid). ABCDEF names them.
lectures.keypoints: B12 stores last 3-4 years, folate 3-6 months. B12 deficiency ↑ methylmalonic acid + homocysteine; folate ↑ homocysteine only — and only B12 gives neurologic signs (proprioception, neuropathy). Megaloblastic film: oval macrocytes + hypersegmented neutrophils; liver disease gives round macrocytes with normal neutrophils. Myeloma and cold agglutinins cause pseudo-macrocytosis.

blocks.html:

  • B12 deficiency
  • Compensatory reticulocytosis
  • Drugs / dysplasia
  • Endocrine (hypothyroidism)
  • Folate deficiency / fetus (pregnancy)

lectures.name: Approach to Hemolytic Anemia
lectures.title: Approach to Hemolytic Anemia
lectures.framing: Hemolysis leaves the same chemical fingerprint whatever the cause; the DAT and the smear then split immune from intrinsic red-cell defects.
lectures.keypoints: Hemolysis = ↑ indirect bilirubin, ↑ LDH, ↑ retics, ↓ haptoglobin. DAT+ IgG = warm (37°C); DAT+ C3 = cold (IgM, Mycoplasma/mono). DAT− with bite cells/Heinz bodies = G6PD (fava, sulfa, antimalarials); with spherocytes = HS (band 3 flow). Mechanical valves and MAHA give schistocytes; PNH is PIGA, not immune. Oral iron: retics in 1 week, stores in 3-6 months.

blocks.html:
Anemia
  • Anemia: Hb below the laboratory reference range for age and sex (by inference ↓ RBCs)
  • Reference: men 135-170 g/L; women 115-160 g/L
Hemolytic anemia
  • Lysis of RBCs; can be microcytic, normocytic or macrocytic depending on the cause
  • Destroyed RBCs release heme (degraded to bilirubin by the reticuloendothelial system), globin, and iron (taken up by the RES, stored as ferritin or hemosiderin)
  • Lab signature: ↑ indirect (total) bilirubin, ↑ LDH, ↑ reticulocytes, ↓ haptoglobin

lectures.name: Myelodysplastic Syndrome
lectures.title: Myelodysplastic Syndromes and Iron, Folate and B12 Metabolism
lectures.framing: MDS is a clonal marrow failure that makes cells badly and can become AML; the second half covers how the marrow's raw materials — iron, folate and B12 — are absorbed, stored and used.
lectures.keypoints: MDS: elderly (median 65-70), cytopenias, AML risk, staged by IPSS; higher risk → hypomethylating agents; del(5q) → lenalidomide. Hepcidin blocks ferroportin. Ferritin = stores; chelate if > 1000. B12: IF in duodenum, absorbed in ileum, stores 3-5 years; folate stores 3-4 months. B12 serves both methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase — folate only the first.

blocks.html:
Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS)
  • Group of clonal hematopoietic stem cell malignancies: ineffective hematopoiesis in ≥ 1 lineage, peripheral cytopenias, and risk of transformation to AML
  • 3-4 per 100,000; far more common in the elderly (1 in 1000); median age 65-70
  • Etiology: idiopathic, or secondary to toxins (chemotherapy, radiation, environmental); may accompany a hereditary disorder or acquired mutations
  • Presentation: anemia (80% at diagnosis, normocytic or macrocytic), neutropenia (40%), thrombocytopenia (30%), progression to AML
  • Ix: CBC (cytopenias), ferritin (iron overload), BM aspirate/biopsy, flow cytometry, cytogenetics
  • IPSS (International Prognostic Scoring System): BM blast %, chromosomal abnormalities, number of cell lines involved
  • MDS with del(5q): < 10% of MDS → macrocytic anemia + thrombocytosis; treat with lenalidomide (Revlimid)

Iron metabolism
  • 20 mg of iron recycled daily to make new RBCs; only 1-2 mg/day absorbed and lost
  • Molecular iron is insoluble and free ionic iron is toxic → carried in blood bound to transferrin
  • Iron is the centre of heme; defective heme-synthesis enzymes cause porphyria
  • Ferritin: storage protein of 24 identical subunits forming a hollow shell; holds up to 4500 iron ions
  • Heme iron: taken up by heme carrier protein (HCP)
  • Non-heme iron (Fe3+) → reduced to Fe2+ by duodenal cytochrome B (helped by ascorbic acid) → taken up by divalent metal transporter (DMT1)
  • Exported from the enterocyte by ferroportin + hephaestin; hepcidin blocks ferroportin when iron is too high

Folate (vitamin B9) metabolism
  • 400 μg/day needed; liver stores (10-12 mg) last 3-4 months
  • Complete dietary lack takes months to cause deficiency — healthy adults store 500-20,000 μg
  • Folate → tetrahydrofolate (THF) (irreversible): cofactor in DNA synthesis (uracil → thymine)
  • 5-methyl-THF → THF (irreversible) by methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR)
  • Methionine synthase: homocysteine → methionine (methylation)
Cobalamin (vitamin B12) metabolism
  • 1-2 mcg/day needed; liver stores (2-5 mg) last 3-5 years
  • Free B12 binds intrinsic factor (IF) in the duodenum; the IF-B12 complex is absorbed in the ileum
  • Cofactor in two reactions: methionine synthase (homocysteine → methionine) and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA, TCA cycle)
  • Pernicious anemia: impaired B12 uptake from lack of IF in the gastric mucosa

lectures.name: Approach to a Bleeding Patient
lectures.title: Approach to a Bleeding Patient and Transfusion
lectures.framing: Stabilize first, stop the bleeding, then work out the cause. The history — mucosal vs deep bleeding — points to platelets/vWF versus coagulation factors before any lab result, and transfusion replaces only the component that is missing.
lectures.keypoints: Mucosal = primary hemostasis (platelets, vWD); joints/muscle = secondary (hemophilia). Normal PT/aPTT does not exclude bleeding (vWD, platelets, FXIII). Hemophilia: X-linked, aPTT ↑ PT normal. vWD type 1 → DDAVP. Transfuse RBCs at Hb < 70, platelets at < 10 (50 surgery, 100 neurosurgery); no platelets in TTP/HUS/HIT. blocks.html:
The three steps
  1. Stabilize the patient — ABCs: airway open and protected, breathing, circulation (blood volume)
  2. Deal with the bleeding — identify the cause, stop it, and maintain adequate levels of each blood component
  3. Work up the cause — history, exam, differential, investigations
History — the most important tool

Sets the pre-test probability of a bleeding disorder and separates congenital from acquired causes.

  • Onset: spontaneous, or with hemostatic challenges (dental extraction, surgery, postpartum, vaccination)
  • Location: mucosal → more likely primary; internal/deep → more likely secondary hemostasis defect
  • Pattern: bruises, petechiae, hematomas; duration, severity and cause of each episode
  • Menstrual history
  • What was needed to stop it: local pressure, cautery/packing for nosebleeds, other interventions
  • Symptoms of anemia/iron deficiency (fatigue, prior iron supplements); previous transfusions
  • Medications: antiplatelets, anticoagulants
  • Family history: vWD, hemophilia A/B, HHT, DIC, vitamin K deficiency; ethnicity, consanguinity — no family history does not rule out a congenital disorder
  • Liver disease, kidney disease
Bleeding assessment tools (BATs)
  • Standardized; improve diagnostic accuracy, describe severity, aid communication, predict bleeding risk
  • MCMDM-1 VWD: scored -1 to +4; 5-10 min
  • ISTH BAT: 0 to +4; 20 min; 13 bleeding domains; normal < 4 adult males, < 6 adult females, < 3 children
  • Pediatric Bleeding Questionnaire (PBQ): -1 to 4; positive > 2
Physical exam
  • Petechiae < 2 mm; purpura 3-5 mm; ecchymosis > 5 mm
  • Skin: pallor, jaundice, size/location of bruises, hematomas, telangiectasia
  • Hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy (lymphoproliferative disorders)
  • Joints: range of motion, hypermobility, hemarthrosis (coagulation factor deficiency)
  • Temperature: hypothermia promotes bleeding

lectures.name: Hemostasis
lectures.title: Hemostasis and Coagulation Testing
lectures.framing: Hemostasis runs in four stages — platelet plug, thrombin generation, fibrin stabilization, then inhibition and fibrinolysis — and the lab probes each with a clotting-time test that maps onto the old intrinsic/extrinsic/common scheme.
lectures.keypoints: vWF–GPIb = adhesion; fibrinogen–GPIIb/IIIa = aggregation. TF/VIIa initiates; thrombin amplifies (V, VIII, XI); tenase (IXa+VIIIa) and prothrombinase (Xa+Va) propagate; FXIII cross-links. Vitamin K-dependent: II, VII, IX, X. aPTT = intrinsic + common, PT = extrinsic + common. Mixing study: corrects = deficiency, doesn't = inhibitor. A negative D-dimer rules out VTE; a positive one means little.

blocks.html:
Definitions
  • Bleeding: to emit or lose blood
  • Hemostasis: activation of multiple clotting-system components in response to vessel injury to control bleeding; four stages below
1. Primary hemostasis — vasoconstriction + platelet plug
  • Triggered by vessel-wall injury exposing subendothelial collagen
  • Vasoconstriction at the injury site ↓ flow (reflex neurogenic mechanisms)
  • Adhesion: vWF tethers platelets to collagen via platelet GPIb/IX; platelets also bind collagen directly through other receptors
  • Activation / contraction: shape change (discoid → spheroid), granule secretion, calcium influx; the plug offers a negatively charged phospholipid surface for coagulation factor assembly
  • Thromboxane: arachidonic acid → (cyclooxygenase) → endoperoxides → (thromboxane synthase) → thromboxane A2
  • Aggregation: fibrinogen bridges platelets by binding activated GPIIb/IIIa → platelet plug

blocks.html:
2. Secondary hemostasis — coagulation factors generate thrombin and fibrin

Initiation

  • Tissue factor (TF) released from injured tissue cells, endothelium and monocytes
  • TF + FVIIa form the TF/VIIa complex, which activates a little FIX and FX → a small amount of thrombin
  • FXII and other contact factors play only a minor role (activating FXI)

Amplification

  • Thrombin activates FV → Va, FVIII → VIIIa, FXI → XIa, and more platelets

Propagation

  • TF/VIIa activates FIX; IXa + VIIIa = tenase complex → converts much more FX to Xa
  • Xa + Va + Ca2+ + phospholipid (activated platelets) = prothrombinase complex → prothrombin (FII) to large amounts of thrombin (IIa)
3. Fibrin clot formation and stabilization
  • Thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin monomers, which polymerize into a soluble clot
  • Thrombin activates FXIII, which cross-links fibrin and stabilizes the clot
4. Inhibition — limit thrombin and break down the clot
  • Block initiation: tissue factor pathway inhibitor (TFPI) targets TF-VIIa and Xa
  • Block further thrombin generation: protein C and protein S inactivate FV and FVIII
  • Block thrombin already generated: antithrombin (also binds FIX, X and XI)
  • Fibrinolysis: t-PA converts plasminogen → plasmin, which breaks cross-linked fibrin into D-dimers
  • Brakes on fibrinolysis: TAFI (thrombin-activatable fibrinolysis inhibitor) suppresses plasmin formation; α2-antiplasmin and PAI-1 inhibit plasmin and t-PA

blocks.cap: Cell-based model: TF-VIIa starts it, thrombin feeds back to activate V, VIII and XI, and FXIIIa turns soluble fibrin into cross-linked fibrin.

blocks.html:
Sample collection
  • In vitro, the lab measures the time taken to form a clot
  • Collected in a blue-top tube with sodium citrate, which chelates calcium so the sample does not clot in transit
  • Centrifugation separates plasma from the platelets (the phospholipid source)
Routine tests
  • PT: extrinsic + common pathway deficiencies/inhibitors. Reagent 0.1 mL (thromboplastin + phospholipid + CaCl2) + 0.05 mL plasma at 37°C. Normal 9-15 s; can be normal in mild deficiency
  • INR: standardizes the PT across labs for monitoring vitamin K antagonists; calculated from PT. Normal 0.9-1.1
  • aPTT: intrinsic + common pathway deficiencies/inhibitors. 0.1 mL reagent (contact activator + phospholipid, no tissue factor) + 0.1 mL plasma + 0.1 mL CaCl2 at 37°C. Normal 25-35 s; can be normal in mild deficiency
  • Thrombin time (TT): fibrinogen deficiency/dysfunction or a thrombin inhibitor. 0.1 mL thrombin + 0.2 mL diluted plasma at 37°C. Time is inversely proportional to fibrinogen activity (calibration curve) — longer = less fibrinogen
  • Fibrinogen assay: fibrinogen activity. Low with loss (bleeding), consumption (post-trauma hyperfibrinolysis, DIC), ↓ production (severe liver disease), congenital, dysfibrinogenemia. Acute-phase reactant — may be non-specifically ↑ in inflammation
  • D-dimer: plasmin breakdown products of cross-linked fibrin; qualitative or quantitative (ELISA or latex immunoassay with monoclonal antibodies). Negative rules out VTE; elevated is non-specific (recent surgery/trauma, cancer, infection/inflammation, DIC, elderly, pregnancy)
  • Anti-Xa assay: activity of Xa-inhibiting anticoagulants — heparin, LMWH, fondaparinux, rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban
  • 50:50 mixing study: 1 part patient + 1 part normal plasma. Corrects = factor deficiency; does not correct = inhibitor; partial = multiple deficiencies or inhibitor
Wells criteria for DVT
  • Active cancer
  • Paralysis, paresis or recent immobilization of the legs
  • Bedridden > 3 days or major surgery within 4 weeks
  • Localized tenderness along the deep venous system
  • Entire leg swollen
  • Calf swelling > 3 cm vs the other side (measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity)
  • Pitting edema confined to the symptomatic leg
  • Collateral superficial veins
  • Previous DVT
  • No alternative diagnosis (as likely)

lectures.framing: A bleeding disorder found in adulthood is usually one that was mild enough to be missed, one whose lab values overstate it, or one that was acquired.

blocks.html:
What turns up in adults
  • Mild-moderate congenital phenotypes — severe forms are usually identified earlier in life
  • Congenital deficiencies with clinico-laboratory discrepancy — a low factor level may not confer a severe bleeding phenotype
  • Acquired bleeding disorders — acquired hemophilia A, acquired vWD, platelet disorders

lectures.framing: A newborn's hemostatic system is still maturing, so normal neonatal coagulation values are not adult values.
lectures.keypoints: Hemostasis matures over the first 6 months. An immature liver means lower vitamin K-dependent factors, protein C and protein S, so PT and aPTT are physiologically longer in neonates and premature infants — interpret against age-specific ranges.

Neonatal hemostasis
  • Hemostatic system matures over the first 6 months of life
  • Liver immaturity → lower levels of most factors: vitamin K-dependent factors, protein C, protein S
  • PT and aPTT are physiologically longer in premature infants and neonates than in adults

lectures.framing: A low platelet count is sorted by mechanism — made too few, destroyed, pooled, or miscounted. The destructive causes split on whether they bleed or clot, which is why several of them must never be given platelets. The lecture then covers the anticoagulants and VTE.

lectures.framing: A high white count is sorted by which lineage, how mature, and whether it is clonal. The clonal mature myeloid disorders are the MPNs, most driven by a JAK2 switch stuck "on".

lectures.name: Approach to Leukopenia
lectures.title: Leukopenia and Febrile Neutropenia
lectures.framing: Neutropenia is graded by the ANC and matters because of infection risk; its most urgent form, febrile neutropenia, is treated as an emergency before the source is known.
lectures.keypoints: ANC < 1.5 = neutropenia; < 0.5 severe. Acquired causes: infection, drugs (chemo, clozapine, antithyroid), autoimmune (Felty), B12/folate/copper, marrow failure, spleen. lectures.framing: Leukemias are classified on two axes — myeloid vs lymphoid and acute (blasts) vs chronic (mature cells) — and the acute ones bring their own emergencies: APL bleeding, tumour lysis and leukostasis.

lectures.framing: One marrow sample feeds four tests — morphology, flow cytometry, cytogenetics and molecular diagnostics — plus a core biopsy for architecture.
lectures.keypoints: Sample the PSIS; never core the sternum. Normal M:E ratio 1:1-3:1; cellularity ≈ 100 − age. Flow: FSC = size, SSC = granularity; needs fresh (< 24 h) sample. Cytogenetics finds chromosome changes; molecular testing finds mutations.

blocks.html:
Morphology of the marrow aspirate
  • Assesses all stages of hematopoiesis
  • Site: posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS); if necessary sternum (children and adults) or tibia (children only)
  • Never take a core biopsy from the sternum (too close to the heart), tibia, skull or ribs
  • Normal aspirate: mixed erythroid and myeloid cells at all stages; myeloid:erythroid ratio 1:1 to 3:1; no dysplasia
Normal core biopsy
  • Subcortical acellular zone often present
  • Cellularity ≈ 100 − age (%)
  • Cell composition similar to the aspirate
Flow cytometry

lectures.framing: Most enlarged nodes are reactive; the job is to use location, character and red flags to find the few that need a biopsy.

blocks.html:
Primary vs secondary lymphoid tissue

Starting a response in the node
  • T cells need an APC (TCR binds peptide-MHC)
  • Immature dendritic cells mature by innate recognition of pathogens, move to the T-cell zone and express CD80/86 (B7.1/B7.2)
  • 3-signal hypothesis: (1) antigen-specific signal (TCR); (2) co-stimulation (CD28 ↔ CD80/86); (3) cytokines
  • B cells become plasma cells: T-independent (low-affinity IgM) or T-dependent (high-affinity)
  • Germinal centre makes high-affinity BCRs by proliferation and somatic hypermutation of the variable region

lectures.name: Multiple Myeloma
lectures.title: Multiple Myeloma and the Mediastinal Mass
lectures.framing: Myeloma is a clonal plasma cell cancer that sits at the far end of a spectrum from MGUS; what separates treatable disease from surveillance is end-organ damage (CRAB). The lecture closes with the approach to a mediastinal mass.
lectures.keypoints: MGUS < 10% PCs, no CRAB (monitor); smoldering ≥ 10%, no CRAB; myeloma = ≥ 10% clonal PCs + CRAB (Ca > 2.52, Cr > 175, Hb < 100, lytic lesions — skeletal survey). Rouleaux, M spike on SPEP/UPEP, free light chains. ISS uses albumin + β2-microglobulin. Cord compression and renal failure are emergencies.   • Each makes one Ig: heavy chain (M, A, D, G, E) + light chain (kappa or lambda)
Multiple myeloma
  • Plasma cell cancer: production and accumulation of non-functional monoclonal antibody (M protein)
  • 1% of malignancies, 13% of hematologic cancers; ~2000 Canadians/year; median age 66; M > F; Black > white

lectures.name: Radiation Oncology
lectures.title: Radiation Oncology, Quality Improvement and Critical Appraisal
lectures.framing: Radiation kills by DNA damage and is given in fractions so normal tissue can recover between doses while tumour cannot. The lecture closes with the QI cycle and the vocabulary of trial appraisal.
lectures.keypoints: Fractionation works through the 4 Rs — repair and repopulation spare normal tissue; redistribution and reoxygenation sensitize tumour. Fast-growing tumours are most radiosensitive. Radiation pneumonitis at 6-12 weeks → steroids; late hypothyroidism, infertility, second cancers. QI: root cause analysis is the forgotten step; outcome/process/balancing measures. ITT is conservative, PP inflates; confounders are not on the causal path; power = 1 − β; NNT = 1/ARR.

blocks.html:
Radiation therapy
  • Ionizing radiation to treat tumours: damages DNA so cells cannot reproduce — normal and cancer cells alike
  • Every tissue has a tolerance dose beyond which damage is irreparable; spinal cord, bowel, kidney and lung are often limiting
  • Delivered externally or internally

rows:

blocks.html:
Fractionation and the 4 Rs
  • Fractionation: total dose split into small daily fractions over weeks
  • Exploits the difference in repair: normal cells recover by repair and repopulation; cancer cells are sensitized by redistribution and reoxygenation and repair less well
  • Cells are most vulnerable in G2-M, when DNA is exposed → fast-growing tumours are more radiosensitive and respond sooner

Critical appraisal — foundations
  • EBM = patient values + clinical expertise + best research evidence
  • Descriptive research: correlational, qualitative (interview), case studies/reports
  • Analytical research: observational (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional); experimental (RCT, non-randomized trial, community trial)
  • Equipoise (ethics of trials): (1) no evidence that any arm is better than another; (2) no evidence that a therapy outside the trial is better than those tested
  • Chance = random error; bias = systematic error. Minimize bias with randomization, double blinding (masking) and intention-to-treat analysis
  • Confounding: an apparently causal exposure-outcome association that is really due to an unconsidered variable. A confounder (1) is a risk factor for the outcome, (2) is associated with the exposure, and (3) is not on the causal pathway
Blinding
  • Outcomes should ideally be assessed blind to treatment assignment
  • Open label: everyone knows the allocation
  • Single blind: patient or clinician unaware
  • Double blind: patient and investigators unaware
  • Triple blind: patient, investigators and analysts unaware
  • Unblinding: disclosure of the allocation
Study protocol components

Background and rationale; objective; design overview and schema; eligibility; enrolment and randomization; treatment regimens; primary and secondary endpoints; clinical evaluations; statistics (sample size, power, analysis plan); data collection; data safety monitoring; plain-language statement and consent form.

Analysis and statistics
  • Intention-to-treat (ITT): analyse by assigned group; everyone randomized is included even if they stopped treatment. De facto standard, required by most journals and regulators; more conservative, reflects the real world
  • Per-protocol (PP): only those who completed the assigned treatment; usually a larger effect estimate, because non-compliers (intolerant or doing poorly) are dropped
  • Non-inferiority margin (delta): the largest loss of efficacy vs control one will accept; pre-specified, from clinical judgement and statistics. A positive NI trial means the new therapy is better than, or no worse than control by more than delta
  • Primary endpoint: main outcome that drives power and sample size; often dichotomous
  • Composite endpoint: ≥ 2 binary endpoints, any one counts; components equally weighted; include the events of interest "and anything worse" (e.g. death) to avoid competing-risk bias
  • p-value usually < 0.05 — look at the population size and event numbers per group; confidence interval usually 95%
  • One-sided test: difference expected in one direction (smaller sample); two-sided: direction unknown
  • Type I error (α) = false positive; type II error (β) = false negative; power = 1 − β (probability of detecting a true difference)
  • Subgroup analysis: is the effect consistent across patient types?
